pages.summary: A stopwatch, and the processor time used.
body: `tic` starts the stopwatch and `toc` gives the seconds since. A stopwatch of one's own (`t0 = tic`, then `toc(t0)`) lets several run at once without disturbing each other. `cputime` gives the processor time used so far, which differs from the time on the clock when the program waits, or works on several cores.
syntax: The seconds on a stopwatch of one's own.
The processor time used, in seconds.

examples.title: A computation timed
examples.intro: The times differ from run to run, so the example shows what they are, not their values.

pages.summary: Waiting: for a number of seconds, or for a key.
body: `pause(s)` waits s seconds (fractions too) and lets the page draw what it has to; `pause` with no input waits until a key is pressed in the Command Window. For a player or recorder of sound, `pause(player)` stops it where it is, and `resume` goes on.
syntax: A player or recorder stopped where it is.

examples.title: An animation drawn step by step
examples.intro: Each pause gives the page time to draw the new frame.

pages.summary: The date and time now: as a vector, a serial date number, and text.
body: `clock` gives [year month day hour minute seconds] (the seconds with their fraction), `now` the serial date number (days from the year 0, the time as a fraction) and `date` today's date as 'dd-mmm-yyyy'. All three are the computer's local time. `datetime('now')` gives the same moment as a datetime.
syntax: Year, month, day, hour, minute, seconds.

examples.title: The same moment three ways
examples.intro: The values change with the time the example is run; the checks show how they agree.

pages.summary: Dates and times as serial numbers, as vectors, and as text.
body: A serial date number counts days from the year 0 (1 January of year 0 is day 1), with the time of day as a fraction: differences are days, and adding 1 is the next day. `datenum` makes them from years, months, days (and hours, minutes, seconds; months and days past their ends roll over), from date vectors or from text; `datevec` gives [year month day hour minute seconds]; `datestr` gives text, in a numbered format (0 to 31) or a pattern of `yyyy`, `yy`, `mmmm`, `mmm`, `mm`, `dd`, `ddd`, `HH`, `MM`, `SS`, `FFF` and `PM`. Datetimes do the same work with time zones and formats of their own.
syntax: n = datenum(Y, M, D, h, m, s)
From [year month day hour minute seconds].
[Y, M, D, h, m, s] = datevec(t)

pages.summary: Days of the week, the ends of months, leap years and a month's calendar.
body: `weekday` gives 1 for Sunday to 7 for Saturday, and the day's short name; `eomday` the last day of a month (29 for February in a leap year); `leapyear` whether a year is one (divisible by 4, except centuries not divisible by 400). `calendar` gives a month as a 6-by-7 matrix, weeks from Sunday to Saturday with 0 outside the month, and prints it when there is no output.
syntax: The day of the week, and its name.
The last day of a month.
A month's days in a matrix.

pages.summary: Serial date numbers moved by calendar amounts; the seconds between two date vectors.
body: `addtodate` adds whole years, months, weeks or days, or hours, minutes, seconds or milliseconds, to serial date numbers (a month later is the same day of the next month). `etime` gives the seconds from one date vector (as `clock` gives) to another.
